newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ's Shipley favours float or partial float of GPS.
newsitem.headline: NZ's Shipley favours float or partial float of GPS.

text.p: State-Owned Enterprises Minister Jenny Shipley said on Wednesday she would prefer a float or partial float of Government Property Services (GPS).
"I personally favour a partial float, if not a full float, for New Zealanders," Shipley told parliament's finance and expenditure select committee.
But she said she would reserve the right to take a different view on other asset sales.
In the June budget the government said it would investigate the sale of GPS and its portfolio of buildings, mainly housing state agencies.
"Probably one of the most challenging questions we will have to face is whether to sell it as one or allow New Zealanders to take a stake in a property company," Shipley said.
She said that would include a decision on whether buildings such as the one housing the security service would be included in any sale.
In 1996 the government called off the sale of the bulk of GPS's portfolio, valued at about NZ$160 million net, citing inadequate offers, but had excluded key government buildings from the sale.
Shipley said the government now intended to have the process completed before the 1998 budget.
"I would think toward the end of the year it will be much clearer what our intentions are," she said.

The coalition has said it would also look at privatising Vehicle Testing New Zealand, wbich tests cars for their warrants of fitness, but has ruled out the sale of six strategic assets, including NZ Post and energy generators ECNZ and Contact Energy.
It said it would assess other state asset case by case.
Shipley said on Wednesday there were other assets "either parts of state-owned enterprises or whole SOEs that the government may in the future wish to reconsider".

"Let me give you an illustration. TVNZ has shares in (telecommunications company) Clear. Whether or not it is appropriate to hold shares in Clear, which are clearly of value, will be an issue the company will wish to argue on the one hand and a future government may wish to argue on the other," Shipley said.
She said if businesses were considered non-core then cabinet would look at whether it should ask SOEs to divest them.
"In general if there were to be any rules, it is that we don't want SOEs (if they are seeking to expand) doing that which the private sector can do equally or better."
She said there was more reluctance by the government to allowing capital expenditure offshore beyond merely the sale of expertise.
NZ Post's bid for a 30 year concession to Argentina's national postal service ENCOTESA was a good example of a case where ministers would have to weigh up the proposal's merits.

"That is mainly weighing up the taxpayers interest ... not trying to pass judgement on the directors' competence, but rather whether or not further exposure on behalf of the New Zealand taxpayer was warranted when that taxpayer may equally want capital that's available to be used for other purposes," Shipley said.
